name: Jamal Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jamal, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lectures take up Monday to Thursday, mostly electronics, a maths module and a programming course in Java that I find a bit tedious. I do my homework in the library until it closes, then walk back to my flat across a bridge with four others, all engineers. Friday evenings I go home on the bus to help in my parents' noodle restaurant. They own it, and I fold dumplings for four hours and get paid in leftover soup.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents wanted something stable, and honestly so did I. Restaurants taught me early that income can swing, and I wanted a profession with a certificate. I had top school results and got a place at a good university, and my parents cover the fees and my flat. I don't use AI tools, because I'd rather learn it properly, and I don't trust answers I can't check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no surprise there. Every few years something is going to change everything, and it mostly doesn't. I'd tell my flatmates to do the work and not worry about predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. The restaurant carries on, my degree stays worth what my parents think it's worth, and I'd have a normal career ahead. I'd still keep an eye on prices, because the restaurant lives on thin margins and rent keeps going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: study, work Fridays at the restaurant, and look for an internship at an electronics firm next summer. I'd not try new tools unless the course forced me to. I'd also ask my father to show me the accounts, so I know how things run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels normal, and I like normal. Boring is a good thing when your family has a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the restaurant something you'd want to take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My dad would like it, but I see how many hours he works. I'd rather have a job with fixed hours and give my parents a hand with the paperwork. They'd retire in about ten years and that's a different decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the prices you keep an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rice, oil, and the electricity bill. When oil goes up ten percent, my dad grumbles for a week and raises the soup price by fifty cents. Customers notice and some stop coming. I think about that a lot more than I think about AI.

say: I'd say every few years something is going to **change everything**, and it mostly doesn't.
I'd tell flatmates to do the work and skip the **predictions**.
think: I feel **fine**, since my degree stays worth what my parents think.
I still watch **prices**, because the restaurant lives on thin margins.
do: Study, work **Fridays** at the restaurant and look for an electronics internship.
Ask my father to show me the **accounts**.
Avoid new **tools** unless the course forces them.
feel: **Normal**, and I like normal, since boring is good for a family business.
S0.quote: Boring is a good thing when your family has a business.
fieldNote: Resistant to change by temperament; sees **hype** cycles as routine.
His real concern is the family restaurant's margins, not AI.
Money is secure, so calm is earned here.

steps.text: Apply for an electronics firm internship next summer
Ask his father to go through the restaurant accounts
Keep working Friday evenings at the restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say things will change but people shouldn't panic. Some jobs shrink and some grow, and that's how it has always been. I'd tell my parents the restaurant should be fine, since people still want dumplings made by a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be more concerned. A lot of what I'm learning in programming is the thinking work on that card, and I don't use any tools, so I'd feel a step behind. My degree is hardware-leaning, which helps, but I can't pretend it doesn't touch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course and put more weight on the hardware modules. I'd try the AI tools once I see which ones my lecturers say are reliable, not before. I'd ask older students what companies actually do, and keep my Friday restaurant shifts, because it's real income if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncomfortable, like when a road you walk every day gets dug up. You can get around it, but you don't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the reliable tools. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people copy something wrong and not notice. If three lecturers recommend a tool, I'll use it, but I won't chase the newest thing. That's how I am, and it's cost me a little but saved me from mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your parents' restaurant started struggling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more shifts, cut my own spending, and try to find a part-time job that pays better. I wouldn't ask them for more money. They already pay for my flat, and I feel that every month.

say: I'd say things will change but nobody should **panic**.
I'd tell my parents people still want dumplings made by a **person**.
think: I'm more **concerned**, since much of my programming is that thinking work.
I feel a step **behind** because I use no tools.
do: Put more weight on the **hardware** modules.
Try AI tools only once lecturers call them **reliable**.
Keep my Friday **restaurant** shifts as real income.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like a road you walk daily being dug up.
S1.quote: If three lecturers recommend a tool, I'll use it, but I won't chase the newest thing.
fieldNote: Waits for **proof** before adopting tools; he knows it costs him a little.
Feels guilt about his parents paying for his flat and would cut his own spending first.
Public calm to his parents, private concern about the programming side of his course.

steps.text: Take extra hardware modules and skip pure software options
Try one AI tool once three lecturers recommend it
Keep Friday evening shifts at the restaurant for income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can't be true as stated, or if it is, governments are far behind and nobody can handle it. I'd say my parents should hold onto cash and not take new loans, because I don't think anyone knows where this is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid. The thinking jobs vanish within two years, and I'd be a second-year student with no experience. Robots for hands-on work take three more years, so my parents' restaurant lasts a while, but the ordering, booking and delivery apps around it change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents to cut costs and not expand. I'd look for any job I could do alongside study, especially hands-on work. I'd try to learn some electrical installation, which people will pay for, and I'd stop spending on anything extra. I wouldn't know whether to finish the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like stepping on a stair that isn't there. I'd have trouble sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you aren't sure about finishing the degree, what would decide it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the companies I'd apply to are still hiring juniors. If the signs are bad after a year, I'd switch to an apprenticeship for electricians. My parents wouldn't love it, but they've seen restaurants close, so they'd understand security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about this with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. My dad doesn't like it when I say things sound bad. I'd say we should keep a bigger cash reserve and keep my fees paid early, and I'd save the scarier thoughts for my flatmate Dani and for you.

say: I'd tell my parents to hold **cash** and avoid new loans while nobody knows where this goes.
I'd say governments are far **behind** and nobody can really handle this.
think: I'd be **afraid**: thinking jobs vanish in two years and I'd have no experience.
Delivery and booking apps around the **restaurant** change at once.
do: Tell my parents to **cut costs** and not expand.
Learn electrical **installation**, which people pay for.
feel: Like stepping on a **stair** that isn't there, and not sleeping.
S2.quote: My parents wouldn't love it, but they've seen restaurants close, so they'd understand security.
fieldNote: Retreats to **security**: cash, cost cuts and a trade, rather than new ventures.
Hides the worst thoughts from his father and keeps them for his flatmate and the interviewer.
Anxious but not alarmed, because family money and his trade fallback give some control.

steps.text: Ask parents to keep a bigger cash reserve and pay fees early
Learn electrical installation basics in evenings
Switch to an electrician apprenticeship if junior hiring dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to think carefully and not rush. I'd tell people to learn useful skills and not follow whoever shouts loudest online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy, but more steady. I'd graduate in three years right in the middle, which is the part I'd dislike. But five years means I can add hardware experience and a trade-adjacent qualification, and my parents will have time to adjust the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, aim for something hardware-heavy like power systems, and take a summer job with an electrical contractor. I'd also put away part of my Friday pay every month. I'd still avoid AI tools until the course requires them, but I'd learn them by third year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for a storm that you can see on the horizon. You have time to close the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your plans differ from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not panic about leaving the degree. With two years I'd think about an apprenticeship now. With five I can finish and add things. I'd also be calmer with my parents, and we could plan around the restaurant's costs over years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools by third year. Why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then they'd be standard and tested. I like to arrive when the path is paved. I know that's not very exciting, but I haven't been wrong yet by doing it that way.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **think** carefully and not rush.
I'd tell people to learn useful **skills** and ignore online shouting.
think: I'm **uneasy** but steadier, since I'd graduate right in the middle of it.
Five years lets my parents **adjust** the restaurant.
do: Aim for **hardware-heavy** work like power systems.
Take a summer job with an **electrical contractor**.
Save part of my Friday **pay** each month.
feel: Like watching a **storm** on the horizon with time to close the windows.
S3.quote: I like to arrive when the path is paved.
fieldNote: The **time** lets him wait for proven tools, which suits his resistant style.
Does not panic about the degree; adds practical skills instead.
Self-aware about being unexciting but proud that it has worked so far.

steps.text: Choose power systems modules for the final two years
Work a summer with an electrical contractor
Save a fixed share of Friday restaurant pay monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can go differently from what people predict. I'd tell my flatmates to enjoy university and not plan around a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Ten years takes me through the degree and a first job, and I'd have time to see which way things go before I'd have to choose. I'd keep my parents' situation in mind, since they'd be near retirement by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, finish the degree, find a stable job at an engineering firm, and help my parents sort out what to do with the restaurant. I'd start saving from my first salary and buy nothing big for the first couple of years. I'd learn the AI tools when they're ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels almost like nothing. Which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your parents' restaurant over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them decide whether to sell it while it's worth something, or hand it to my cousin who's keen on running it. I'd not take it on myself. I'd also try to make sure they've got enough savings, because that's where I can help most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind that it's far away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw big engineering firms stop hiring graduates for a full year, or if a robot started doing the kitchen jobs in the next restaurant chain. Ordinary signals like that I'd trust more than a news story.

say: I'd say a lot can go **differently** from what people predict.
I'd tell flatmates to enjoy university and not plan around a **headline**.
think: I'd be **fine**, with time to see which way things go.
My parents will be near **retirement** by then.
do: Finish the degree and find a **stable** job at an engineering firm.
Help my parents decide whether to **sell** the restaurant.
Save from my first salary and buy nothing **big** early on.
feel: Almost like **nothing**, which is how I like it.
S4.quote: Ordinary signals like that I'd trust more than a news story.
fieldNote: Calm, with a clear idea of what **signals** would change his mind: hiring freezes and kitchen robots.
Sees the restaurant as his parents' retirement question, not his own career.
Consistent resistant style: he wants proof, not forecasts.

steps.text: Finish the degree and target a stable engineering firm job
Help parents decide whether to sell the restaurant
Save from the first salary and avoid big purchases

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time to check anything. What would help is plain information from universities about which jobs are still hiring, plus a safety net for families like mine who live on small business income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't loud, but we notice. I don't use the tools and I don't plan to jump first. I'd just like to be treated as someone who's thinking, not as someone who's behind.

headlineQuote: I'd just like to be treated as someone who's thinking, not as someone who's behind.
portrait: Jamal is an 18-year-old **electronic engineering** student whose parents run a noodle restaurant and pay his fees and flat.
He is pragmatic and cautious: he doesn't use AI tools and adopts things only once they are proven.
He leans on **trade skills** and a stable career as his safety net, and works Fridays at the restaurant.
His real worries are family margins, prices and his parents' retirement, more than AI itself.
He is calm in the quiet pictures, uneasy in the middle, and **anxious** in the two-year picture.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it leaves no time to check anything.
whatWouldHelp: Plain information on which jobs are **hiring**, and a safety net for small-business families.
